176.title: Vayera: visiting the sick (Genesis 18:1)
176.hook: God appears to Abraham as he heals; the rabbis learn that God visits the sick (Sotah 14a)
176.tomorrow: Vayera: shall not the judge do justly?
176.howItsDone: Visiting the sick is a mitzvah in Jewish law; many synagogues have bikur cholim volunteers who visit hospitals and homes, and the Mi Sheberach prayer for healing is said during the Torah reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, new names: Abram became Abraham, Sarai became Sarah, and the covenant of circumcision began. Your line was a name can grow. Today, a new portion: Vayera. Day one hundred seventy-six.

When someone's sick, most of us freeze a little. We don't know what to say. We don't want to intrude. Maybe they want rest. Maybe we'll catch something. So we send a text, a heart emoji, get well soon, and feel slightly guilty. The fourth portion of the Torah opens with a single quiet verse: God appears to Abraham, sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day. It doesn't say why. But the rabbis looked at where this verse sits, right after Abraham's circumcision, and drew a conclusion that became a whole Jewish practice. Today's word is that practice.
screen: `WE DON'T KNOW WHAT TO SAY.` → `A TEXT, A HEART EMOJI.` → `GOD APPEARS AT THE TENT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Vayera, and he appeared, from its first verse: "And the LORD appeared unto him by the terebinths of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." Why does God appear? No message is given. No command. Just presence. The rabbis noticed that the verse right before tells of Abraham's circumcision, at ninety-nine. So Abraham is recovering, sore, sitting in the shade. The Talmud says God came to visit the sick, to ask after his welfare. Then the Talmud builds a whole teaching on it. The Torah says to walk after the LORD your God. How can a person walk after God? By copying God's ways. God clothed the naked, Adam and Eve. So you clothe the naked. God visited the sick, Abraham. So you visit the sick. God comforted mourners, Isaac after his father died. So you comfort mourners. God buried the dead, Moses. So you bury the dead. The Hebrew for visiting the sick is bikur cholim. Bikur means a visit, and cholim are the sick. It's a mitzvah, a commandment, and many Jewish communities have a bikur cholim committee whose whole job is to show up. The Talmud even says a visitor takes away a small part of the illness, one sixtieth. It's not medicine. It's company. And the rabbis offer practical advice: don't visit so early or so late that you tire the person out; sit at their level; pray for them, if you pray. Just by showing up, the story says, you're doing what God did at a tent door on a hot day.
screen: `AND THE LORD APPEARED UNTO HIM.` · `AFTER THE CIRCUMCISION, HEALING.` · `WALK AFTER GOD: CLOTHE, VISIT, COMFORT.` · `ONE SIXTIETH OF THE ILLNESS.` · then, large: `VISIT THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with someone who's unwell, in your mind first. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's sick, or hurting, or recovering, near or far. Picture yourself sitting beside them, at their level, not standing over them. You don't need to say anything clever. Just be there. If you pray, you can ask for their healing. If you don't, just hold them in mind with warmth. Then decide how to reach them for real. The bell holds the time.
Bikur cholim. Visiting the sick: a Jewish commandment learned from God, who appeared to Abraham as he healed.
Your line: visit the sick. Today, visit or call one person who's unwell. Not a text. Your voice, or your face. Day one hundred seventy-six.

screen: `DAY 176 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: VAYERA: SHALL NOT THE JUDGE DO JUSTLY?`

fork.reveal: show up: not too early, not too long, sitting at their level. that's bikur cholim, and it's what God did at the tent door.

trapdoor: what you thought: God came to Abraham to deliver a message.
what it means: God simply appears to Abraham while he heals, and the rabbis learn that visiting the sick is walking in God's ways.
what a scholar hears: Sotah 14a (Rabbi Chama bar Chanina on Deuteronomy 13:5); Bava Metzia 86b (third day after the circumcision); Nedarim 39b–40a (one sixtieth; guidance for visitors).

177.title: Vayera: shall not the judge do justly? (Genesis 18:25)
177.hook: Abraham asks "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?"
177.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often point to Abraham's plea for Sodom as the model for arguing with God on behalf of justice, a thread that runs through the prophets, the Psalms and Hasidic stories.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bikur cholim: God appeared to Abraham as he healed, and visiting the sick became a way of walking after God. Your line was visit the sick. Who did you call? Day one hundred seventy-seven.

Have you ever had to push back on someone with far more power than you? A boss. A judge. A doctor. A parent, when you were young. Your heart pounds. You choose every word carefully. You say, with respect, I don't think that's fair. Now imagine pushing back on God. That's exactly what happens in this portion. Three visitors have eaten at Abraham's tent and are heading toward Sodom. And God decides to tell Abraham what's about to happen to that city. What Abraham does next is one of the boldest things anyone says in the whole Torah. Today.
screen: `PUSHING BACK ON POWER.` → `THE VISITORS HEAD TOWARD SODOM.` → `ABRAHAM PUSHES BACK ON GOD.`

segments.voice: First, God asks, almost to himself: "Shall I hide from Abraham that which I am doing?" And decides not to, because Abraham is meant to teach his children to do righteousness and justice. So God says: the outcry from Sodom is great, and its sin is very grievous. And Abraham steps forward. Would you destroy the righteous with the wicked? What if there are fifty righteous people in the city? That be far from you. And then the line: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" Think about who he's saying it to. And God agrees: for fifty, I'll spare the whole place. Then Abraham keeps going. He says: I, "who am but dust and ashes," what if there are forty-five? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Ten? Each time, God says yes. Abraham stops at ten. The story leaves it there. Notice three things. First, Abraham is arguing for strangers. Sodom isn't his city. Its king is the one whose wealth he refused. He argues for them anyway. Second, he's humble and bold at once: dust and ashes, and still asking. Third, God doesn't rebuke him. The conversation is almost invited. God told Abraham so that he'd speak up. Jewish tradition has made room for this ever since: prophets, psalmists and rabbis who argue with God, and in Hasidic stories too, a rebbe who calls God to a trial on behalf of his people. Arguing for justice, even with heaven, isn't the opposite of faith. In this story, it's what faith sounds like.
screen: `SHALL I HIDE FROM ABRAHAM?` · `WHAT IF THERE ARE FIFTY?` · `DUST AND ASHES, AND STILL ASKING.` · `ARGUING FOR STRANGERS.` · then, large: `JUSTICE, EVEN FROM GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the fifty. Settle, and breathe. Think of a group you're tempted to write off completely: a city, a crowd, the other side of an argument. Now ask Abraham's question: are there fifty good people there? Forty? Ten? Picture even one of them, going about an ordinary day. Let them be real to you. Then think of one small way you could speak up for fairness. The bell holds the time.
Vayera. The portion where God appears to Abraham, and Abraham argues for a city of strangers: shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?
Your line: justice, even from God. Today, speak up for fairness once, respectfully, even when the person in charge outranks you. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

178.title: Vayera: Abimelech (Genesis 20)
178.hook: a foreign king turns out more upright than Abraham feared
178.howItsDone: Jewish commentators read Genesis 20 as a story in which Abraham's fear of strangers proves mistaken, and note that it is the first place the Torah calls anyone a prophet and describes a person praying for someone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vayera, Abraham argued for a city of strangers: shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly? Your line was justice, even from God. Today, Abraham misjudges some strangers himself. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

You move to a new town, or start a new job, or travel somewhere far away. And before you've met anyone, you've already decided a few things about them. People here are cold. People here can't be trusted. Better keep your guard up. Sometimes that instinct protects you. And sometimes it's just wrong, and the people you braced against turn out to be decent, even better than you. Abraham, the great hero of this portion, the one who just argued for strangers, walks into a foreign town with exactly that fear. Today, what he assumed, and what he found.
screen: `BEFORE YOU'VE MET ANYONE.` → `KEEP YOUR GUARD UP.` → `ABRAHAM WALKS INTO GERAR.`

segments.voice: Abraham and Sarah travel to Gerar, ruled by a king named Abimelech. And Abraham tells people Sarah is his sister, not his wife. So Abimelech, thinking she's unmarried, takes her into his house. That night God comes to Abimelech in a dream and warns him: she's a married woman. And Abimelech, who hasn't touched her, protests. He asks God, in effect, will you destroy even a righteous nation? He said she was his sister. She said he was her brother. I did this with a clean heart and clean hands. Listen to that question. It's almost Abraham's own words from the day before, shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly, now in the mouth of a foreign king. And God agrees: I know you did this with a clean heart; that's why I kept you from sinning. Return her. And the text adds something: Abraham is a prophet, and he'll pray for you. It's the first time the Torah calls anyone a prophet. In the morning Abimelech returns Sarah, gives gifts, and says to Abraham: my land is before you; live wherever you like. Then he asks the obvious question: why did you do this to me? And Abraham answers honestly: "Surely the fear of God is not in this place." He assumed these people had no conscience. He was wrong. The king he feared turned out to be decent, and fair, and generous. And Abraham prays for Abimelech's household, and they're healed. The father of the Jewish people learns, in his own story, that goodness isn't only found at home.
screen: `SHE IS MY SISTER.` · `A CLEAN HEART AND CLEAN HANDS.` · `NO FEAR OF GOD IN THIS PLACE.` · `ABRAHAM PRAYS, AND THEY'RE HEALED.` · then, large: `GOODNESS IS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: undo one assumption. Settle, and breathe. Think of a group of people you've quietly decided lack goodness: another neighborhood, another country, another party, a kind of person who annoys you. Notice the assumption, without judging yourself for it. Then picture one of them doing something decent: returning what isn't theirs, keeping a promise, being kind. Let that picture be as real as the fear. The bell holds the time.
Vayera. The portion where Abraham fears a foreign king, and the king turns out more upright than he feared.
Your line: goodness is everywhere. Today, catch yourself assuming the worst about a stranger, and look for one sign of goodness instead. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: Vayera: Isaac is born (Genesis 21:1–7)
179.hook: God remembers Sarah, and she says all who hear will laugh with her
179.howItsDone: Genesis 21 is read in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, when, tradition says, Sarah was remembered; the birth of Isaac is often taught alongside Sarah's two laughs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a foreign king turned out more upright than Abraham feared. Your line was goodness is everywhere. Where did you find some? Today, a promise twenty-five years long comes true. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

There are two kinds of laughter. One is the laugh when someone tells you something impossible. Oh, sure. Right. A short, dry laugh that means: that'll never happen. The other is the laugh that bursts out of you when the impossible thing happens anyway. The baby is born. The test comes back clear. The person you gave up on walks through the door. It's the same sound, almost, but it comes from a completely different place. Sarah laughs both ways in this portion. Today, the second laugh.
screen: `OH, SURE. RIGHT.` → `THE IMPOSSIBLE HAPPENS ANYWAY.` → `SARAH LAUGHS BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: A few chapters back, three visitors came to Abraham's tent, and one of them said: this time next year, Sarah will have a son. Sarah was listening from inside the tent. She was about ninety. And she laughed to herself: after I'm worn out, and my husband is old, shall I have pleasure? And God asked Abraham: why did Sarah laugh? "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" Sarah, afraid, said, I didn't laugh. And the answer came back: no, you did laugh. That was the first laugh. Now, chapter twenty-one. The Torah says God remembered Sarah, as promised, and did for her as God had spoken. She conceives and gives birth to a son, in her old age, at exactly the time foretold. Abraham names him Yitzchak, Isaac, which means he will laugh. And Sarah says: God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh with me. Then she says, almost in wonder: who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? The laugh has turned inside out. The same word, from disbelief to joy. And notice: she doesn't keep it. Everyone who hears will laugh with me. Rashi, following the midrash, says that when Sarah was remembered, many other childless women were remembered with her, many sick people were healed, many prayers were answered, and there was laughter in the whole world. This chapter is read in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah. The tradition says Sarah was remembered on that day. At the start of every Jewish year, the story of a laugh that turned from doubt to joy.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHED TO HERSELF.` · `IS ANY THING TOO HARD FOR THE LORD?` · `YITZCHAK: HE WILL LAUGH.` · `LAUGHTER IN THE WHOLE WORLD.` · then, large: `LAUGH WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a laugh of joy. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time something you'd given up on actually happened, big or small. Remember the laugh, or the smile, that came out of you. Let it come back into your face now, even a little. Then picture the people you'd want to share it with. Everyone who hears will laugh with me. Let the joy spread out to them. The bell holds the time.
Vayera. The portion where Sarah's laugh of disbelief becomes a laugh of joy, and her son is named Isaac, he will laugh.
Your line: laugh with me. Today, share one good thing with someone and laugh together about it, out loud. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

180.title: Vayera: here am I (Genesis 22:1, 7, 11)
180.hook: Abraham answers "here am I" to God, to his son and to the angel
180.tomorrow: Chayei Sarah: the life of Sarah
180.howItsDone: The binding of Isaac, the Akedah, is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and many Jews recite it in the daily morning prayers; hineni is also the name of a prayer the cantor says before the Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur services in many communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaac was born, and Sarah's laugh turned from doubt to joy. Your line was laugh with me. Who did you laugh with? Today, the last day of Vayera, and its hardest chapter. Day one hundred eighty.

Someone calls your name from the next room. You say: yeah? What? In a minute. Half your mind is still on what you were doing. Now think of the few times you answered a call with all of you. A child crying at night, and you're up before you're awake. A friend on the phone, and you can hear that something's wrong, so you put everything down. There's a word in Hebrew for answering like that. It's not just yes. It means: I'm here, fully. Abraham says it three times in one chapter. Today's word.
screen: `YEAH? WHAT? IN A MINUTE.` → `ANSWERING WITH ALL OF YOU.` → `ONE WORD, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: The word is hineni. Here I am. The chapter is Genesis twenty-two, which Jews call the Akedah, the binding of Isaac. It's one of the hardest stories in the Torah, and Jews have wrestled with it for centuries. It begins: "God did prove Abraham, and said unto him: 'Abraham'; and he said: 'Here am I.'" Then God tells him to take his son, his only son, whom he loves, Isaac, and offer him up on a mountain. Abraham rises early and goes. On the third day, father and son walk up the mountain together, Isaac carrying the wood. And Isaac speaks: "My father." And Abraham says: "Here am I, my son." The same word. Isaac asks where the lamb is, and Abraham says God will provide. Then, at the top, when Abraham has bound Isaac and raised the knife, an angel calls from heaven: Abraham, Abraham. And a third time he answers: here am I. And the angel says: don't lay your hand on the boy. Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it instead. Isaac is not harmed. Readers disagree deeply about this story. Many see Abraham's complete faith. Others read it as the Torah's way of rejecting child sacrifice, which other peoples of the time practiced. Some midrashim wonder whether Abraham should have argued, as he did for Sodom. All of them notice the word. Hineni, to God. Hineni, to his son. Hineni, to the angel who stops him. Fully present to each. Later, when God calls, the prophet Isaiah will answer: "Here am I; send me." So that's Vayera: a visit to the sick, an argument for justice, a stranger's goodness, a laugh of joy, and here am I.
screen: `GOD CALLS: HERE AM I.` · `ISAAC CALLS: HERE AM I, MY SON.` · `THE ANGEL CALLS: HERE AM I.` · `READERS DISAGREE DEEPLY.` · then, large: `HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say here I am, and mean it. Settle, and breathe. Silently say: here I am. Notice where you actually are: your body, this room, this moment. Then think of someone who might call your name today, a child, a parent, a friend, a coworker. Picture answering them not with in a minute, but with all of you: here I am. If you pray, you can say it to God too. The bell holds the time.
Hineni. Here I am: not just yes, but fully present, Abraham's answer to God, to his son, and to the angel.
Your line: here I am. Today, when someone calls your name, put down what you're holding, turn, and answer with all of you. Day one hundred eighty.

screen: `DAY 180 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CHAYEI SARAH: THE LIFE OF SARAH.`

181.title: Chayei Sarah: the life of Sarah
181.hook: a portion called "the life of Sarah" begins with her death
181.howItsDone: Chayei Sarah is read in synagogues each autumn, and many Jews remember loved ones by telling stories of their lives at shivah, the week of mourning, and on each yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hineni: Abraham answering here I am, to God, to his son, to the angel. Your line was here I am. Who did you show up for? Day one hundred eighty-one.

Think about the last funeral you went to. At some point, someone stood up and said: let's not talk about how she died. Let's talk about how she lived. The stories came out. The way she laughed. The thing she always cooked. This week's Torah portion does the same thing, in its name. It's called Chayei Sarah, the life of Sarah. And its very first lines tell us that Sarah has died. Every week, Jews read a portion named for her life that opens with her death. Today: why the name is life.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE SAY AT A FUNERAL.` → `CHAYEI SARAH: THE LIFE OF SARAH.` → `IT OPENS WITH HER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Portions take their names from their first important words, and here the first words are these. In the Jewish Publication Society's old translation: "And the life of Sarah was a hundred and seven and twenty years; these were the years of the life of Sarah." Notice it doesn't say Sarah died at a hundred and twenty-seven. It says her life was that long, and then it says so again. The Hebrew counts it strangely, too: a hundred years, and twenty years, and seven years, each with its own word for years. Rashi, the great medieval teacher, read that slowly. He said each stage of her life is counted on its own because each was whole. At a hundred she was as free of wrongdoing as she had been at twenty, and at twenty as lovely as at seven. And then that closing phrase, these were the years of the life of Sarah: Rashi says all of them were equally good. Not only the famous ones. The waiting years, the laughing year, the old years. There's a harder side, too. The portion comes right after Abraham takes Isaac up the mountain, and an old midrash connects the two: Sarah died, it says, when she heard what had happened to her son. The text itself is silent about that. What the text does say is that Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her. So the portion holds both things. A real death, real grief, and a name that points past it. The rabbis loved that choice. When you remember someone, you get to choose which word goes on the door. The Torah chose life.
screen: `THE LIFE OF SARAH WAS…` · `A HUNDRED, TWENTY AND SEVEN YEARS.` · `ALL HER YEARS WERE GOOD.` · `ABRAHAM CAME TO MOURN AND WEEP.` · then, large: `THE PORTION IS CALLED LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a life, not just a death. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've lost, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even a pet. Let yourself skip past the ending for a moment. Find one ordinary scene from their life. A kitchen. A car ride. Something they always said. Stay in that scene. Let them be alive in it for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Chayei Sarah. The life of Sarah: a Torah portion that opens with her death, and is named for her life. Chayim, life, is the same word in the toast l'chaim.
Your line: the portion is called life. Today, tell someone one story about a person you miss, a story from their living, not their dying. Day one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: Chayei Sarah: a fair price (Genesis 23:3–20)
182.hook: a grieving stranger negotiates with respect for a grave
182.howItsDone: Jewish law gives great weight to honest business, from fair weights and measures to not misleading a buyer, and the cave of Machpelah in Hebron is still visited as the burial place of the patriarchs and matriarchs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chayei Sarah: a portion named for her life. Your line was the portion is called life. This week ran from Abraham visited as he healed, through justice, a surprising king, a baby's laugh and here I am, to a funeral. Today, the grave itself. Day one hundred eighty-two.

Picture Abraham the morning after. His wife has died. He's old, he's grieving, and he has a problem nobody talks about until it happens: where do you bury someone? He has lived in this land for decades, and he doesn't own a single square foot of it. So he walks to the town gate, where business gets done, and stands in front of the people of Heth, the locals. A mourner, asking strangers for a favor. Today: how you buy a grave with honor.
screen: `THE MORNING AFTER.` → `NOT ONE SQUARE FOOT HIS OWN.` → `A MOURNER AT THE TOWN GATE.`

segments.voice: Abraham opens with a line that's almost painful. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I am a stranger and a sojourner with you." A foreigner who lives here. Give me a burial place, he says, so I can bury my dead. The locals are gracious. You are a prince of God among us, they say, bury your dead in the best of our graves. Abraham bows to them. Twice, the text says, he bows to the people of the land. He has one cave in mind, the cave of Machpelah, at the edge of a field owned by a man named Ephron. And he asks for it at full price. The Hebrew says kesef malei, full silver. Ephron answers, in front of everyone: no, my lord, I give it to you. The field and the cave, a gift. It sounds generous. Abraham bows again, and says no. Let me pay. Then Ephron names a number, almost in passing: land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Four hundred shekels is a lot of money. Abraham doesn't haggle. He weighs out the silver, at the merchant's standard, in front of witnesses. The rabbis noticed something small. After the deal, Ephron's name is spelled with one letter missing, and Rashi says that's because he talked big and did little. Abraham, meanwhile, never took the free gift. Why? Commentators give reasons: a gift can be taken back, and a grave is forever. A purchase in front of witnesses is clean. And this cave, bought with full silver, becomes the first piece of the land the family owns. Sarah is buried there. Later, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah too.
